questions.stem: Which of the following is an abiotic component of a freshwater stream ecosystem?
options: The dissolved oxygen concentration of the water
The algae growing as a film on submerged rocks
The bacteria breaking down fallen leaf litter
The mayfly nymphs sheltering under stones
questions.explanation: Abiotic components are the non-living physical and chemical features of an environment, such as dissolved oxygen, temperature and pH. Algae, bacteria and mayfly nymphs are all living, so they are biotic components even though they live in close contact with the water and rocks.

questions.stem: An abiotic factor that is in shortest supply relative to an organism's needs, and so restricts the growth of its population, is called:
options: a tolerance range
a trophic level
an ecological niche
a limiting factor
questions.explanation: A limiting factor is whichever resource or condition most restricts growth, such as phosphate in a lake or water in a desert. A tolerance range is the span of conditions in which an organism can survive, which is related but describes the organism rather than the scarce resource.

questions.stem: A mayfly nymph survives in water between 5 °C and 20 °C and is most abundant near 12 °C. A shallow, unshaded stretch of a creek reaches 24 °C every summer afternoon. What would you predict for this stretch?
options: Mayfly numbers will rise, since warm water holds more oxygen
Mayfly nymphs will be rare or absent there in summer
Mayfly nymphs will be most abundant there in summer
Mayfly numbers will be unaffected, since temperature is biotic
questions.explanation: 24 °C lies outside the species' tolerance range of 5–20 °C, so few or no nymphs would be expected there. Warm water actually holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water, which would add to the stress rather than relieve it.

questions.stem: A student fills two open flasks with the same tap water and leaves them, without any organisms, until they reach equilibrium with the air: one at 10 °C and one at 25 °C. Which result is expected?
options: The 10 °C flask has the higher dissolved oxygen concentration
The 25 °C flask has the higher dissolved oxygen concentration
Both flasks have the same dissolved oxygen concentration
Neither flask contains any oxygen, as no plants are present
questions.explanation: The solubility of oxygen in water falls as temperature rises, so cooler water holds more dissolved oxygen at equilibrium with air. Oxygen dissolves from the air by diffusion, so water holds oxygen even when there are no photosynthesising organisms in it.

questions.stem: A tall eucalypt canopy shades the forest floor, keeping it cooler, damper and more humid than an open paddock nearby. This is best described as:
options: an abiotic component altering the biotic conditions of a microhabitat
a limiting factor acting on the producers of the open paddock
a food web interaction between the canopy and the forest floor
a biotic component altering the abiotic conditions of a microhabitat
questions.explanation: The canopy trees are living (biotic) and they change the light, temperature and humidity (abiotic) beneath them, creating a distinct microhabitat. The reverse wording fails because light and humidity are the factors being changed, not the cause of the change.

questions.stem: Introduced common carp stir up sediment as they feed, making lake water turbid. Native submerged plants then decline. Which description fits this sequence best?
options: A mutualism forms between carp and the turbidity-tolerant plants
The carp compete directly with submerged plants for dissolved oxygen
A biotic factor changes an abiotic factor, which then limits producers
An abiotic factor changes a biotic factor, which then limits consumers
questions.explanation: The carp (biotic) increase turbidity (abiotic), which reduces the light reaching submerged plants, the producers. The reversed chain gets cause and effect the wrong way round: turbidity is the result of the carp feeding, not its cause.

questions.stem: Dissolved oxygen in a small, plant-filled farm dam is logged every hour for two days. It peaks in the late afternoon and is lowest just before dawn. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?
options: Respiration only happens in daylight, so oxygen use stops at night and peaks again during the afternoon
Wind mixes oxygen into the water only at night, which is why the lowest values are recorded in the afternoon
Photosynthesis adds oxygen faster than respiration uses it in daylight; at night only respiration occurs
Water is warmest just before dawn, so it holds the least oxygen then, and cooler afternoon water holds the most
questions.explanation: By day, photosynthesis by plants and algae releases oxygen faster than all organisms consume it, so dissolved oxygen builds up until late afternoon. At night photosynthesis stops but respiration continues, so oxygen falls until dawn. Water is usually coolest, not warmest, just before dawn, so temperature cannot explain the minimum.

questions.stem: In summer a deep lake forms a warm surface layer that does not mix with the cold bottom layer. By late summer, water near the lake bed is almost without oxygen. What is the best explanation?
options: Oxygen is less dense than water, so it rises to the surface and leaves the bottom layer over summer
Decomposers use oxygen near the bed, and the layering stops oxygen-rich surface water mixing down
Cold water holds less dissolved oxygen than warm water, so the bottom layer naturally loses its oxygen
Photosynthesis by rooted plants on the dark lake bed consumes oxygen faster than it can be replaced
questions.explanation: Bacteria decomposing organic matter that sinks to the bed consume oxygen, and while the lake is stratified no oxygen-rich surface water is mixed down to replace it. The cold-water explanation reverses the solubility relationship: cold water can hold more oxygen, not less.

questions.stem: Fungi and bacteria that secrete enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorb the products are best described as:
options: detritivores
producers
primary consumers
decomposers
questions.explanation: Decomposers digest dead matter externally with secreted enzymes and absorb the products, releasing nutrients back to soil and water. Detritivores such as earthworms and slaters also feed on dead matter, but they ingest it and digest it internally.

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, which organism is the secondary consumer?
options: Frog
Grasshopper
Snake
Grass
questions.explanation: The grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the primary consumer and the frog, which eats the primary consumer, is the secondary consumer. The snake is the tertiary consumer because it eats the secondary consumer.

questions.stem: On average, about what percentage of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next trophic level?
options: About 10%
About 50%
About 90%
About 100%
questions.explanation: Roughly 10% of the energy at one level is stored in the biomass of the next; the rest is lost mainly as heat from respiration, or in faeces and uneaten parts. About 90% is the proportion lost, not the proportion passed on.

questions.stem: A food web differs from a food chain because a food web:
options: shows the total biomass present at each of the trophic levels
shows the energy lost as heat at each step of the transfer
shows only the producers and herbivores of the community
shows many interconnected feeding relationships in a community
questions.explanation: A food chain is a single pathway of feeding, while a food web links many food chains to show that most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one species. Biomass at each level is shown by a biomass pyramid, not by a food web.

questions.stem: Producers in a grassland capture 50 000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Assuming 10% transfer between trophic levels, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
options: 5000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹
50 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹
500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹
5 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹
questions.explanation: Primary consumers receive 5000, secondary consumers 500 and tertiary consumers 50 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹, as each step keeps 10%. 500 is the energy reaching the secondary consumers, which comes from stopping one step early.

questions.stem: In a paddock, primary consumers take in 2000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the secondary consumers that eat them take in 150 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. What is the efficiency of this energy transfer?
questions.explanation: Efficiency is energy at the higher level divided by energy at the lower level: 150 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 7.5%. Dividing the other way gives 13.3, and 92.5% is the proportion of energy not passed on.

questions.stem: Why is a pyramid of energy for an ecosystem never inverted?
options: Energy is lost as heat at each transfer, so every level has less than the level below
Consumers are always larger organisms than producers, so they hold more energy each
Biomass always increases up the trophic levels, so energy must decrease to balance it
Producers store their energy for many years, so they always hold the largest amount
questions.explanation: Each trophic level can only receive energy from the level beneath it, and most of that energy is lost as heat from respiration, so energy must decrease at every step. Biomass pyramids can be inverted, as in some oceans, but energy pyramids cannot.

questions.stem: In an open-ocean ecosystem, the biomass of phytoplankton present at any one time is smaller than the biomass of the zooplankton that graze on them. Which explanation is correct?
options: Energy increases at each trophic level in the ocean, so the zooplankton level holds more biomass
Phytoplankton obtain their energy from the zooplankton, so they always have less biomass
Phytoplankton reproduce so fast that a small standing biomass supports a large flow of energy
Zooplankton are producers that photosynthesise as well as graze, so they hold extra biomass
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid shows only the mass present at one moment. Phytoplankton divide rapidly and are eaten quickly, so a small standing crop has a high turnover and still passes more energy upward than the zooplankton hold. Energy itself still decreases at each level, so the energy pyramid stays upright.

questions.stem: A single river red gum supports 3000 caterpillars, which are eaten by 40 birds. How would the pyramids of numbers and biomass for this food chain compare?
options: Numbers pyramid is upright; biomass pyramid has a narrow base of one tree
Both pyramids have a narrow base, because only one tree is present
Both pyramids are upright and identical, because they show the same chain
Numbers pyramid has a narrow base of one tree; biomass pyramid is upright
questions.explanation: Counting organisms gives 1 tree, 3000 caterpillars and 40 birds, so the numbers pyramid has a narrow base. The one tree has far more mass than all the caterpillars, which outweigh the birds, so the biomass pyramid is upright.

questions.stem: In a woodland, foxes eat rabbits and small ground-nesting birds, rabbits graze native grasses, and the birds eat insects. If foxes were removed by a baiting program, which short-term change is most likely?
options: Bird numbers fall, because the birds lose the predator that eats them
Insect numbers rise, because more insect-eating birds are now present
Rabbit numbers rise, increasing grazing pressure on native grasses
Rabbit numbers fall, because the rabbits lose part of their food source
questions.explanation: With their predator removed, rabbits survive and breed in greater numbers and graze the grasses more heavily. More birds would mean more insects eaten, so insect numbers would be expected to fall, not rise.

questions.stem: Mycorrhizal fungi grow in and around eucalypt roots. The fungi supply the tree with phosphorus from the soil and receive sugars from the tree. This relationship is an example of:
options: competition
mutualism
parasitism
commensalism
questions.explanation: Both partners benefit, the tree gaining phosphorus and the fungus gaining sugars, which defines mutualism. In parasitism one partner benefits at the other's expense, and in commensalism one benefits while the other is unaffected.

questions.stem: A herbivore eats 1000 kJ of plant material. It loses 400 kJ in faeces and 500 kJ through respiration. How much energy is available to the next trophic level from its new biomass?
options: 500 kJ
900 kJ
100 kJ
600 kJ
questions.explanation: Only energy stored in new biomass is available to the next level: 1000 − 400 − 500 = 100 kJ. 600 kJ is the energy absorbed, before the 500 kJ used in respiration is subtracted.

questions.stem: Which of Earth's four systems includes the soils, rocks and minerals of the crust?
options: Atmosphere
Lithosphere
Hydrosphere
Biosphere
questions.explanation: The lithosphere is the solid Earth, including rock, minerals and soil. The hydrosphere is all of Earth's water, the biosphere is all living things and the atmosphere is the layer of gases around Earth.

questions.stem: Which process moves carbon from the atmosphere into the biosphere?
options: Cellular respiration
Combustion
Decomposition
Photosynthesis
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, producers take in carbon dioxide from the air and build it into glucose and other organic compounds. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all do the opposite, releasing carbon dioxide back to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Transpiration moves water between which two of Earth's systems?
options: From the biosphere to the atmosphere
From the atmosphere to the biosphere
From the hydrosphere to the lithosphere
From the lithosphere to the hydrosphere
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plant leaves through the stomata, so water moves from living plants (biosphere) to the air (atmosphere). Water entering plants from the air would be the reverse, which is not transpiration.

questions.stem: Which process converts atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia that plants can use?
options: Ammonification
Nitrogen fixation
Nitrification
Denitrification
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, including those in the root nodules of legumes and wattles, convert N₂ into ammonia. Ammonification also produces ammonia, but from the nitrogen in dead organic matter, not from the gas in the air.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes energy and matter in ecosystems?
options: Energy and matter are both recycled between living and non-living parts
Energy is recycled by decomposers, while matter is lost as heat
Energy and matter both flow one way and are lost from the system
Energy flows through and is lost as heat, while matter is recycled
questions.explanation: Energy enters as sunlight, passes along food chains and leaves as heat, so it must be constantly resupplied. Atoms such as carbon and nitrogen are reused over and over through cycles. Decomposers recycle nutrients, not energy.

questions.stem: Which pair of processes both return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
options: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
Photosynthesis and sedimentation
Combustion and ocean absorption
Cellular respiration and combustion
questions.explanation: Respiration by living things and the burning of fuels or vegetation both release carbon dioxide into the air. Photosynthesis and ocean absorption remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, so any pair containing them is wrong.

questions.stem: Unlike the carbon and nitrogen cycles, the phosphorus cycle:
options: depends on bacteria fixing phosphorus from the air
takes place only within the hydrosphere
does not pass through any living organisms
has no significant phase as a gas in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Phosphorus cycles mainly through rocks, soil, water and living things, and is released slowly by the weathering of rock. It has no important gaseous form, so there is no atmospheric store or fixation step as there is for nitrogen.

questions.stem: Waterlogged paddock soil steadily loses its nitrate. Which process is mainly responsible?
options: Nitrogen fixation by bacteria converting nitrate to nitrogen gas
Ammonification by fungi converting nitrate to organic nitrogen
Denitrification by anaerobic bacteria converting nitrate to nitrogen gas
Nitrification by aerobic bacteria converting nitrate to ammonia
questions.explanation: In waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil, denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen and release nitrogen gas to the atmosphere. Nitrification needs oxygen and runs the other way, turning ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate.

questions.stem: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide and forms weak carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves limestone and forms caves. Which interaction between Earth's systems does this show?
options: The atmosphere and hydrosphere acting on the lithosphere
The lithosphere and biosphere acting on the atmosphere
The biosphere and hydrosphere acting on the atmosphere
The lithosphere acting on the hydrosphere and biosphere
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolves in water from the hydrosphere, and the resulting acid weathers rock, which is part of the lithosphere. No living organisms are needed for this chemical weathering.

questions.stem: Gases from an explosive eruption reach the stratosphere, and global average surface temperature dips for the following year or two. Which interaction between Earth's systems explains the dip?
options: Lithosphere to atmosphere: sulfate aerosols formed from sulfur dioxide reflect sunlight
Lithosphere to atmosphere: carbon dioxide from the eruption absorbs incoming sunlight
Hydrosphere to atmosphere: steam from the eruption forms clouds that trap outgoing heat
Biosphere to atmosphere: forests burnt by lava release smoke that blocks the sunlight
questions.explanation: In the stratosphere, sulfur dioxide from the eruption forms tiny sulfate aerosol droplets that reflect incoming sunlight, so the surface cools until they settle out after a year or two. Volcanic carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that would warm rather than cool, and the amount from one eruption is small.

questions.stem: A patch of eucalypt forest is cleared and the timber burnt. Which description of the carbon movement is correct?
options: Carbon moves from the lithosphere to the biosphere as the ash is absorbed by new seedlings
Carbon moves from the hydrosphere to the atmosphere as the water in the timber evaporates
Carbon moves from the biosphere to the atmosphere, and future uptake by photosynthesis falls
Carbon moves from the atmosphere to the biosphere, and future uptake by photosynthesis rises
questions.explanation: Burning releases the carbon stored in the trees' biomass as carbon dioxide, and with the trees gone the site removes less carbon dioxide by photosynthesis. Evaporating water from the timber moves water, not carbon.

questions.stem: In terms of energy and matter, planet Earth is best described as:
options: closed to both energy and matter
closed to energy but open to matter
open to energy but essentially closed to matter
open to both energy and matter
questions.explanation: Earth receives energy from the Sun and radiates heat to space, so it is open to energy. Apart from small amounts such as meteorites and gases lost to space, its matter stays on Earth and is recycled, so it is essentially closed to matter.

questions.stem: In a systems model of a farm dam, rainfall entering the dam is classified as:
options: an output
a component
a store
an input
questions.explanation: An input is matter or energy that enters the system from outside, as rain does. Evaporation or water pumped out would be outputs, and the stored water and the dam's clay lining are components.

questions.stem: In a systems diagram of a farm dam, which of these is a process rather than a component?
options: The water held in the dam
The clay lining of the dam
The reeds along the dam's edge
Evaporation from the water surface
questions.explanation: A process is an action that moves or transforms matter or energy, such as evaporation, infiltration or photosynthesis. The stored water, the lining and the reeds are all parts of the system, which makes them components.

questions.stem: A feedback loop that reduces the original change and returns a system towards its earlier state is called:
options: an amplifying loop
a reinforcing loop
a negative feedback loop
a positive feedback loop
questions.explanation: Negative feedback counteracts a change and helps keep a system stable. Positive feedback, also called amplifying or reinforcing feedback, makes the original change larger.

questions.stem: Warming melts Arctic sea ice, exposing darker ocean that absorbs more sunlight, which causes further warming and more melting. In systems thinking, this is:
options: a negative feedback loop that reduces the warming
a negative feedback loop, because the ice re-forms
not a feedback loop, because no output affects an input
a positive feedback loop that amplifies the warming
questions.explanation: The output of the change, less ice, feeds back to cause more of the same change, which is positive feedback. Negative feedback would counteract the warming, but here each step reinforces it.

questions.stem: Which process in a forest system is invisible to the human eye without instruments?
options: Run-off flowing across the soil surface after heavy rain
Trees being blown over during a severe storm
Diffusion of carbon dioxide into leaves through the stomata
Leaves falling from the canopy onto the forest floor
questions.explanation: Systems thinking includes processes that are invisible, such as gas exchange at the stomata, which can only be detected with instruments such as gas analysers. Leaf fall, run-off and windthrow can all be seen directly.

questions.stem: A student models a wetland as a system. Which list correctly sorts these items: inflowing creek water, the sediment on the bed, denitrification, and water seeping into the groundwater?
options: Input; process; component; output
Output; component; process; input
Input; component; process; output
Component; input; output; process
questions.explanation: The creek water enters from outside (input), the sediment is a part of the wetland (component), denitrification transforms nitrate within it (process), and seepage to groundwater leaves the wetland (output). A common error is calling the sediment a process because things happen in it.

questions.stem: Which sampling technique is best suited to estimating the density of a plant species spread evenly across a large grassland?
options: Kick sampling
Randomly placed quadrats
Mark-recapture
Pitfall traps
questions.explanation: Quadrats placed at random give an unbiased sample of a stationary organism's density. Mark-recapture is for mobile animals, pitfall traps catch ground-dwelling invertebrates and kick sampling is used for stream invertebrates.

questions.stem: To describe how plant species change from a lake's edge up the slope to dry woodland, the most appropriate sampling method is:
options: a single large quadrat at the midpoint of the slope
a belt transect from the water's edge up the slope
random quadrats placed across the dry woodland only
mark-recapture of plants along the shoreline
questions.explanation: A transect samples along an environmental gradient, here from wet to dry, so it shows how species change with distance from the water. Random quadrats in one zone, or a single quadrat, cannot show a change along the gradient.

questions.stem: Five 1 m² quadrats contain 4, 7, 3, 6 and 5 saltbush seedlings. Estimate the number of seedlings in a 200 m² area of the same habitat.
questions.explanation: The mean is (4 + 7 + 3 + 6 + 5) ÷ 5 = 5 seedlings per m², so 5 × 200 = 1000. Using the total of 25 instead of the mean gives 5000, and using the largest count of 7 gives 1400.

questions.stem: Students mark 40 skinks and release them. A week later they capture 50 skinks, of which 10 are marked. Using the Lincoln index, estimate the population size.
questions.explanation: Population = (number first marked × total in second capture) ÷ marked recaptures = 40 × 50 ÷ 10 = 200. Adding 40 and 50 gives 90, which ignores the proportion of marked animals recaptured.

questions.stem: In a mark-recapture study, some of the paint marks rubbed off the skinks before the second capture. What effect does this have on the population estimate?
options: It underestimates the population, because more unmarked animals are counted
It overestimates the population, because fewer marked animals are recognised
It underestimates the population, because fewer marked animals are recognised
It has no effect, because the second sample size stays the same
questions.explanation: Lost marks make the number of recognised recaptures smaller, and since it is the divisor in the Lincoln index, the estimate becomes too large. The sample size is unchanged, but the fraction that appears marked falls, which inflates the result.

questions.stem: Adding phosphate to tanks of lake water greatly increased algal growth, but adding nitrate to identical tanks did not. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Light rather than any nutrient was limiting the algae's growth
Phosphorus was the limiting nutrient for the algae in that water
Nitrogen was the limiting nutrient for the algae in that water
The algae do not require nitrogen to grow and reproduce
questions.explanation: Growth rose only when phosphate was added, so phosphorus was the factor in shortest supply. The algae still need nitrogen; there was simply already enough of it in the water. If light were limiting, adding phosphate would not have increased growth.
